title: How do you load-test a service and set capacity limits?
description: From realistic workloads to saturation curves: choosing tools, finding the knee point, and turning results into limits, autoscaling rules, and SLOs.

data.text: **Question:** How do you load-test a service and set capacity limits?

Model a **realistic workload** (mix of endpoints weighted by production traffic, realistic payloads and think-time, plus the auth/data paths), run it with a tool like **k6, NBomber (.NET), Gatling, or Locust**, and ramp load gradually while watching latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), error rate, and resource saturation (CPU, DB connections, pool exhaustion). The goal is the **knee point**: the throughput level where p99 bends upward — that's your per-instance capacity. Set **limits below the knee with headroom** (e.g., ~60–70% of it): max RPS per instance, autoscaling thresholds, rate-limit quotas per client, and connection-pool sizes. Always soak-test for leaks (memory, connections) and spike-test for cold-start behavior; a single burst test lies about steady-state capacity.

items: Workload realism: weight endpoints by real traffic (usually a few hot GETs dominate), use production-like data volumes — testing against an empty DB measures nothing
Closed vs open models: closed (VUs think between requests) models interactive users; open (constant arrival rate) models the real world at overload — use open for capacity, closed for UX
Ramp stages: baseline → gradual ramp to find the knee → step beyond to see failure mode → soak at target → spike
Metrics triad: latency percentiles (never averages), error rate, saturation (CPU, thread-pool starvation, DB pool wait time, GC pressure)
The knee: throughput plateaus while p99 climbs — beyond it you're queueing, not serving; capacity = knee, not max
Limits from evidence: instance capacity × safety factor = autoscale target; DB pool = instances × per-instance concurrency cap — the classic hidden ceiling
NBomber/k6 specifics: NBomber runs in-process .NET with real HttpClient; k6 uses JS scenarios and has great metrics/stages; both feed Prometheus
Post-test: profile the bottleneck (dotTrace/MiniProfiler/DB plan), fix, re-run — capacity testing without a bottleneck story is just theater

data.title: k6 stages and turning the knee into limits

items: Testing against an empty dev database — data volume and index stats change everything
Using average latency — p99 hides the users you lose
One 5-minute burst and calling it capacity — no soak, so leaks and pool drift stay hidden
Load-testing auth with cached tokens or skipping login — the hottest path goes untested
Ignoring the load generator itself — a laptop can't drive 50k RPS; distribute generators
Setting autoscale on CPU only — saturation often appears in pool wait/queue depth first

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Realistic mix, production-like data, open-model arrival rates
The knee (p99 bend) is capacity — set limits and autoscale below it with headroom
Soak for leaks, spike for cold starts; watch percentiles, errors, saturation
Results drive concrete numbers: per-instance RPS, pool sizes, rate-limit quotas
data.takeaway: Capacity is a measured number, not a vibe: find the knee with a realistic ramp, then set every limit in the system deliberately below it.
